risks.note: China accounts for over 96% of total global solar glass capacity. Following anti-dumping duties on solar glass imports from China and Vietnam in December 2024, import patterns shifted rather than stopped — production has increasingly moved to Malaysia and Indonesia, which are not currently subject to such duties. Management also flags trans-shipment through Southeast Asian hubs and inventory dumping as practices that may undermine trade protections, distort pricing and disrupt fair competition, and the possibility that Chinese manufacturers set up production facilities in other countries to access key markets like India.
risks.risk: Competition from dumped/low-priced Chinese solar glass and duty circumvention through third countries

risks.note: Management states that policy and regulatory developments remain critical, as shifts in incentives or compliance requirements may directly influence pricing, project economics and profitability. Structural support currently comes from ALMM, Basic Customs Duties and the anti-dumping/countervailing duties the Company championed; timely policy intervention is repeatedly cited as necessary to safeguard domestic manufacturers, including against surplus Chinese capacity being redirected to India during prolonged US-China tariff tensions.
risks.risk: Dependence on policy and trade-remedy support; adverse shifts in incentives or compliance requirements

risks.note: Within the solar glass sector, the emergence of integrated players with captive capacities creates the risk of sporadic supply of surplus production entering the open market, triggering price-based competition and margin pressures. Management separately notes that as large players increasingly shift toward captive consumption, surplus capacities are driving pricing pressures alongside aggressive tariff bidding.
risks.risk: Emergence of integrated module players with captive solar glass capacity

risks.note: Capacity in upstream segments such as polysilicon, ingots and wafers remains non-existent in India and continues to evolve; any gaps in these critical inputs could expose the sector to supply chain disruptions and pricing pressures, particularly from Chinese suppliers. Management expects ingot and wafer exposure to ease over the next 2-3 years as new capacities are set up, but states the threat still continues in the case of polysilicon — relevant because ALMM List-III will require domestic wafers and ingots by 2028.
risks.risk: Missing upstream domestic value chain (polysilicon, ingots, wafers) exposing the sector to input supply and pricing shocks

risks.note: The Company's operations are focused on a single primary business segment, the manufacture of flat glass, with no separate reportable segments under Ind AS 108; revenue is disclosed only on a geographical basis. Earnings therefore track one product's pricing cycle, which is the same cycle exposed to import dumping and captive-capacity surplus.
risks.risk: Single-product, single-segment concentration in flat (solar) glass

risks.note: In Europe, policy implementation gaps have led to the closure of several module manufacturing facilities as cheap imports of solar modules flood the markets, weakening competitiveness. This is a direct demand risk for the Company's European furnace, and Europe/Turkey lead its exports. In the United States, trade tensions intensified in April 2026 with triple-digit anti-dumping duties (123.04%) on solar imports from India and Southeast Asian hubs.
risks.risk: Weak European module manufacturing base undermining the Company's European operations

risks.note: Geopolitical risks in the Middle East cause supply chain issues for critical inputs like oil & gas, raise commodity prices, increase freight costs and delay critical component deliveries. Disruptions to critical fuel supply routes have caused problems including escalating prices — material for an energy-intensive furnace operator.
risks.risk: Geopolitical instability in the Middle East disrupting fuel and freight

risks.note: Identified in the BRSR material issues table as a negative-implication risk: any compromise of customer privacy or data security may result in reputational harm, missed business opportunities and increased legal exposure; cybersecurity incidents can interrupt operations, expose sensitive information and lead to financial losses from litigation, regulatory penalties and remediation costs. Cyber Security is among the top enterprise-level risks reviewed by the Board's Risk Management Committee.
risks.risk: Cyber security and data privacy exposure
